context: Hobsbawm studied how traditions presented as long-standing can have relatively recent histories.
opening: The festival claims the ribbon has always been blue. The dyer's oldest bill is for green. The dancers love the blue ribbon dearly.

folds.action: Sew the dated receipt inside the hem
folds.arrival: The dancers can keep the blue and show when the change happened. Someone asks who paid for the first blue dye.

folds.action: Ask three dancers to tie their remembered colours
folds.arrival: The line brightens with incompatible memories. The archive gains a question about when a custom begins.

question: Which part of the dance might the receipt date, and which would need another witness?

name: Gerda Lerner
title: A register of those allowed to sign
context: Lerner developed women's history and examined how historical records can exclude women's experiences.
opening: The volume is full of signatures. A laundress who kept the house running appears only on the washing bill. One shelf has room for both.

folds.action: Bind the bill beside the signatures
folds.arrival: A worker enters the story through payment. The bill still cannot say what she wanted.

folds.action: Reserve an index entry for the missing names
folds.arrival: A future find has somewhere to land. A gap stops looking like an absence of work.

question: What did finding the bill change about the list of people who could sign?

name: Beatrice Medicine
title: The copy that has to come home
context: Lakota anthropologist Beatrice Medicine wrote about fieldwork, language and the responsibilities of an anthropologist working within and across communities.
opening: The field notebook has a neat shelf number. The speaker who corrected my transcription has no copy. We can fix that before the drawer closes.

folds.action: Return a copy with space for corrections
folds.arrival: The speaker can challenge the transcription later.

folds.action: Catalogue the correction beside the first reading
folds.arrival: The archive shows who changed the account.

question: Who can still correct the record once it enters a collection?

name: Marc Bloch
title: Two witnesses, one rumour
context: French historian Marc Bloch helped found the Annales journal and studied how historians compare and interrogate evidence.
opening: Both witnesses give me the same unusual detail. I like agreement. I like independent agreement better. Find out where each first heard it.

folds.action: Draw a chain of transmission
folds.arrival: The two accounts may have a common source.

folds.action: Seek a separately dated record
folds.arrival: A third source can test the timing.

question: What makes two accounts independent?

name: Margaret Mead
title: The audience at the interview
context: Mead studied adolescence in Samoa. Her account and its interpretation have been widely debated.
opening: The visitor asks for one sentence about growing up on an island. A young person speaks differently to a friend than to a visiting adult. Both occasions belong in the record.

folds.action: Restore the interview's audience to the account
folds.arrival: The next reader sees who was listening. A casual answer no longer has to speak for a whole island.

folds.action: Invite separate accounts on the speakers' terms
folds.arrival: The accounts differ. Nobody is asked to perform a culture's single authorised childhood.

question: Who could safely answer with an audience present, and who needed another setting?

name: Derek Freeman
title: The return voyage for a disputed account
context: Freeman disputed Mead's interpretation of her Samoan fieldwork. His critique is also contested.
opening: The archive has two descriptions from different visits. The publisher wants a winner. The dates, speakers and questions do not line up so neatly.

folds.action: Put the dates along the shoreline
folds.arrival: The gap between visits becomes visible. The later account cannot simply erase the earlier setting.

folds.action: Match only interviews with comparable questions
folds.arrival: The comparison shrinks to fewer records. Its remaining disagreement becomes much clearer.

question: Which two accounts could you fairly compare once you lined up their dates?

name: Lewis Binford
title: The ash beside the doorway
context: Binford advocated testing explanations for archaeological patterns against material evidence.
opening: The guide calls every dark patch a hearth. A tidy theory ought to risk losing an argument with this particular floor.

folds.action: Map ash against paths and walls
folds.arrival: One patch lies in a walking lane. That gives the crew a second explanation to examine.

folds.action: Make a prediction for the next patch
folds.arrival: The next patch can count against the hearth story. The guide leaves his old label on a removable clip.

question: Where would you look for ash if the doorway had been used differently?

name: Ahmed Kamal
title: The label with room for a student
context: Ahmed Kamal was an Egyptian Egyptologist who catalogued antiquities and worked to train Egyptian scholars.
opening: The object has a number. My apprentice has copied its signs. If we file only the number, how will the next reader check either of us?

folds.action: File the copy beside the number
folds.arrival: The next reader can compare drawing and stone.

folds.action: Mark the damaged sign before translating
folds.arrival: The uncertainty survives in the translation.

question: Which detail lets another reader challenge a catalogue entry?

name: Mortimer Wheeler
title: A square left standing
context: Wheeler advocated systematic excavation in a grid with baulks that preserved vertical sections.
opening: The team wants the last strip cleared. That strip is also our page of layers. Walk its length before you tell them to lift it.

folds.action: Draw the section before joining the squares
folds.arrival: The interruption remains in the record.

folds.action: Keep a strip for a second reader
folds.arrival: Another observer can check the sequence in place.

question: When is preserving access to evidence worth delaying an investigation?

name: David Graeber
title: The unpaid bowl of soup
context: Graeber examined debt and the social meanings of exchange.
opening: The clerk has called every transfer in the kitchen a sale. A neighbour remembers a gift, a debt and a favour that nobody expected repaid.

folds.action: Give the three bowls different return slips
folds.arrival: A gift comes back without a price. The clerk must say which transfers his ledger measures.

folds.action: Trace one bowl through the next supper
folds.arrival: It changes hands again. What began as help has become an obligation in somebody else's account.

question: Which bowl would lose part of its story if every meal counted as a loan?

name: Friedrich Hayek
title: The price at the far stall
context: Hayek examined how prices convey dispersed information.
opening: The price rises before word of the broken cart reaches the square. A buyer needs the signal now. The carter needs someone to hear why it rose.

folds.action: Pass the changed price down the row
folds.arrival: The next stall adjusts in time. The number travels faster than news of the carter.

folds.action: Pin the carter's message beside the price
folds.arrival: A buyer can judge a local cause. Two outer stalls receive the message after closing.

question: What information reached the far stall before the carter could?

name: Joan Robinson
title: The well with one buyer
context: Robinson analysed imperfect competition, including markets with a single buyer.
opening: The wage board shows that everyone accepted the offered rate. The only other employer lies beyond an impassable ford. The ink has made agreement look effortless.

folds.action: Put the ford on the wage chart
folds.arrival: Readers can see the cost of walking away. Acceptance means something different on this side of the water.

folds.action: Invite a second workshop to post an offer
folds.arrival: Workers gain another figure to compare. Only those able to travel can take it.

question: What other route to work would give a worker a different bargaining position?

name: B. F. Skinner
title: The bell that taught the keeper
context: Skinner studied how consequences affect the likelihood of behaviour.
opening: The bird rings a bell and gets a seed. The keeper hears the bell and gets up every time. Which one has trained the other?

folds.action: Tally the keeper's movements
folds.arrival: The supposedly idle observer has a striking pattern. The bird's part is still visible.

folds.action: Change when the empty bell rings
folds.arrival: Some responses persist after the old pairing stops. The keeper asks how long the observation should last.

question: Which keeper movement might be answering the bell by habit?

name: Ferdinand de Saussure
title: The lecture nobody copied whole
context: Saussure’s posthumously published Course in General Linguistics drew on students’ notes from his lectures.
opening: Three notebooks came out of the same room. The sentence the editor likes appears in only one. Put the pages under glass before we bind them.

folds.action: Show the three pages side by side
folds.arrival: Readers see agreement and gaps.

folds.action: Print the reconstructed sentence with its sources
folds.arrival: The editor’s responsibility is visible.

question: Whose words can a reconstruction claim to preserve?

name: Mary Haas
title: The vowel on the second card
context: Haas documented Indigenous languages of North America, including Tunica, and trained generations of linguists.
opening: The second card sounded like the first until I heard the word in a sentence. Let the speaker finish before you join my two piles.

folds.action: Keep the sentence with the card
folds.arrival: The reader can recover its context.

folds.action: Ask for a contrasting pair
folds.arrival: The distinction can be tested in a new setting.

question: Which difference in sound carries a difference in meaning?

name: Pauli Murray
title: The rule between two index tabs
context: Murray compiled States’ Laws on Race and Color and wrote about the overlapping effects of racial and sex discrimination.
opening: The file clerk can put her complaint under either tab. Read it after you have covered one tab. Now tell me which part of her experience disappeared.

folds.action: Cross-reference both headings
folds.arrival: The complaint can be found from either route.

folds.action: Keep the person’s account beside the statute
folds.arrival: The reader can compare a rule with its effects.

question: What does a filing system make a researcher overlook?

name: Raúl Prebisch
title: The crate that buys fewer tools
context: Argentine economist Raúl Prebisch examined trade between industrial centres and primary-producing economies.
opening: The same number of crates came downriver. The workshop can buy fewer tools. Follow both price labels before you blame the harvest.

folds.action: Compare prices in pairs
folds.arrival: The purchasing power of one crate becomes visible.

folds.action: Add a second trading season
folds.arrival: A single difficult year can be distinguished from a longer tendency.

question: Which comparison explains what the workshop can actually buy?

name: Wassily Kandinsky
title: The chord with no painted violin
context: Kandinsky explored abstract painting and connections between colour and music.
opening: The visitor asks what my blue shape is a picture of. A musician in the doorway has already answered it with a low note.

folds.action: Let the musician answer in sound
folds.arrival: The shape keeps its outline. People disagree about whether the note made it warmer or heavier.

folds.action: Hang the shape without a title for one turn
folds.arrival: Visitors arrange themselves at different distances. The title comes back to a room with several readings.

question: What did the musician add that a title beside the shape would miss?

name: Diego Rivera
title: The wall on the workers' route
context: Rivera's murals often placed working people within public depictions of history.
opening: The patron sees the mural from across the square. Workers pass it at arm's length. They get a shoulder where he gets a scene.

folds.action: Walk the wall at shift change
folds.arrival: The painter finds a detail visible only to someone walking home. The overall composition still belongs to the square.

folds.action: Put a worker's gesture at the corner
folds.arrival: A passer-by recognises a task in a single hand. The distant patron asks why the hand looks so large.

question: What does the worker see on a shift change that a visitor standing still would pass over?

name: Marcel Duchamp
title: The ordinary thing on the plinth
context: Duchamp's readymades included Fountain, the urinal submitted under the name R. Mutt in 1917. The work called attention to the role of selection and exhibition.
opening: A slip about Fountain lies on the plinth. The porter brings an ordinary thing from our cupboard and asks what made a urinal an artwork in that other room. Try a title, or take a turn at arranging the view.

folds.action: Leave the title while the object changes rooms
folds.arrival: The porter follows the title to an empty plinth. A visitor goes looking for the object.

folds.action: Let the porter choose the viewing angle
folds.arrival: From the workbench it looks useful again. A second visitor argues that the choice of angle is part of the work.

question: What changed for the porter when the same object moved rooms?

name: Augusta Savage
title: The sculpture that cannot pay for bronze
context: Savage made sculpture and taught artists during the Harlem Renaissance. Some major works survive through records.
opening: The plaster catches a boy's expression exactly. The commission can pay for an opening but scarcely for a lasting cast. A cheering crowd will not keep plaster dry.

folds.action: Shelter the plaster and invite small groups
folds.arrival: Fewer people see the work today. Tomorrow a young sculptor can study the original surface.

folds.action: Make a record of the work in the square
folds.arrival: The crowd can see it at full scale. The record travels after the fragile material has gone.

question: Who can encounter the sculpture through the square record, and what would they miss?

name: Lygia Clark
title: The hinge a visitor finishes
context: Clark made hinged works called Bichos that viewers could manipulate.
opening: The guard tries to put the hinged sculpture back in its proper shape. The last visitor left it balanced like a small animal waking up.

folds.action: Give the next visitor the hinge
folds.arrival: The shape changes again. The guard begins keeping track of decisions instead of searching for a final pose.

folds.action: Keep one pose until its maker returns
folds.arrival: Another visitor studies the balance. She must wait before discovering what her own hands might make.

question: Whose decision survives if the hinge keeps its last pose overnight?

name: Ousmane Sembène
title: The projectionist's missing voice
context: Sembène made films for African audiences using languages including Wolof.
opening: The reels arrived. The language on the poster belongs to the office that paid for the print. The people outside want to hear themselves in the hall.

folds.action: Host the screening in the audience's chosen language
folds.arrival: The jokes land at different moments. A visitor asks for another way into the dialogue.

folds.action: Pair the screening with a local storyteller
folds.arrival: The teller brings the remote scene close. The director and teller can disagree about what a cut means.

question: Which meaning can change when a storyteller takes part in the screening?

name: Betye Saar
title: The box that looks back
context: Saar's assemblages rework found materials and confront racial stereotypes.
opening: The collector recognises the old advertisement in the box and smiles before seeing what the artist has done to it. There is a moment when the smile changes.

folds.action: Hang the box at the viewer's eye level
folds.arrival: A visitor catches her own expression in the glass. The inherited image is harder to pass without a second look.

folds.action: Show the source image on a separate flap
folds.arrival: The viewer chooses whether to uncover the hurtful original. The transformation in the assemblage has a visible history.

question: What can a viewer learn from opening the source flap after looking into the box?

name: Genesis Breyer P-Orridge
title: The scrape that became a refrain
context: P-Orridge worked across experimental music and performance, including the use of industrial sounds.
opening: The technician marked a scrape as a fault and cleaned it out of the mix. To the performer it was where the room began to sing back.

folds.action: Loop the scrape at rehearsal volume
folds.arrival: The audience hears the rhythm inside a discarded sound. The technician keeps a clean take too.

folds.action: Move the microphone to the listening seats
folds.arrival: The room enters the recording. A perfect repeat of yesterday’s performance is now quite impossible.

question: Whose seat would make the scrape sound like a cue instead of an accident?
